steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on reducing hallucinations in entity abstract summarization. Our framework, SlotSum, generates a template with slots and then fills in the facts; explain the task, the hallucination problem, our approach and new dataset, and list the contributions.

- Prior approaches
  - early work (cite): extractive, select valuable sentences -> poor fluency
  - large-scale WikiSum dataset (cite) -> recent work generates abstractive summaries directly
  - ways to find necessary info in vast inputs:
    - classify documents into topics to filter noisy data (cite)
    - HierSumm (cite): learning-based ranker for input docs + models cross-paragraph dependency

- Problem: hallucinations
  - models can't ensure factual correctness
  - hallucinations = nonsensical / unfaithful contents in generated text (cite)
  - hinder performance, introduce false info in real-world use (cite)
  - Figure 1: Peter Wichers -> band name + genre right, nationality American instead of Sweden
  - misled by snippet "from Atlanta and Baltimore" -> relates it to America
  - such errors hard to detect w/ automatic metrics; degrade performance; fail user expectations (cite)
- Idea: templates + facts-template decomposition
  - hallucination intrinsic to LMs; hard even for LLMs (cite)
  - hard to eliminate under seq2seq; attempts w/ external knowledge: dense retrieval (cite), API calling (cite)
  - templates suit external knowledge: slots guide retrieval
  - templates used in data-to-text (cite), dialogue system (cite); none yet for entity abstract summarization
  - plain text -> hard to locate hallucinations; LM generates semi-structured template before final summary
  - abstract = Facts (factual info about entity) + Template (remaining generic components)
  - -> locate facts easily; correct w/ external knowledge (KB or human assistance)
- SlotSum framework
  - explainable; disentangles facts from generated abstracts to reduce hallucination
  - step 1: template from input docs, facts replaced by slots w/ special tokens
  - step 2: predict facts per slot; rectify w/ credible external knowledge
  - final summary = facts filled into slots
  - ensures factual correctness w/ external knowledge; can still summarize from input docs alone
  - controllable + explainable: facts explicit, easily edited
- Dataset and results
  - WikiFactSum = WikiSum (cite) + related facts
  - SlotSum w/ BART-large backbone (cite) clearly beats baselines on ROUGE given credible external knowledge
  - factual correctness: automatic metrics + human eval -> significantly more correct facts
- Contributions
  - disentangle fact from text in entity abstract summarization -> fewer hallucinations from PLMs
  - SlotSum: templates w/ slots -> predict facts -> correct w/ external knowledge -> fill slots
  - new dataset WikiFactSum + experiments; clear advantage -> disentangling facts gives more factually correct summaries

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Entity abstract summarization is the task of generating a correct and fluent summary of an entity from a collection of relevant documents gathered from the Internet. The task is usually seen as a variant of the multi-document summarization task, as shown in Figure 1. Entity abstract summarization could give users condensed information about a given entity in search engines, and it assists the writing of new Wikipedia entries.

Early work on entity abstract summarization mostly used extractive methods that select valuable sentences from the input documents, and these have the problem that the generated summary has poor fluency. Inspired by the large-scale WikiSum dataset, recent work tends to generate abstractive summaries directly from the input documents. Different approaches have been tried for identifying the necessary information from the vast input documents. One work classifies documents into different topics to filter out noisy data. HierSumm ranks the input documents with a learning-based ranker and models the dependency across different paragraphs. NoisySumm distills the knowledge in a noisy teacher model into a student model.

However these models suffer from hallucinations because they cannot ensure that the generated summaries are factually correct. Hallucinations are the nonsensical or unfaithful contents in generated texts. They can hinder performance and introduce false information in real-world applications. For example in Figure 1, the summarization model gets the band name and band genre of the given entity Peter Wichers right, but it wrongly assumes the nationality is American instead of Sweden. The model is hallucinated by the text snippet “from Atlanta and Baltimore” in the source, and it mistakenly relates this snippet to the nationality of America, ignoring the fact that Peter Wichers comes from Sweden. Factual errors like these are hard to detect with automatic metrics and they can degrade the system performance, which leads to failing to meet user expectations in real-world scenarios.

  - step 2: predict facts per slot; rectify w/ credible external knowledge
  - final summary = facts filled into slots

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Entity abstract summarization is the task of generating a correct and fluent summary of an entity from a collection of relevant documents gathered from the Internet. The task is usually seen as a variant of the multi-document summarization task, as shown in Figure 1. Entity abstract summarization could give users condensed information about a given entity in search engines, and it assists the writing of new Wikipedia entries.

Early work on entity abstract summarization mostly used extractive methods that select valuable sentences from the input documents, and these have the problem that the generated summary has poor fluency. Inspired by the large-scale WikiSum dataset, recent work tends to generate abstractive summaries directly from the input documents. Different approaches have been tried for identifying the necessary information from the vast input documents. One work classifies documents into different topics to filter out noisy data. HierSumm ranks the input documents with a learning-based ranker and models the dependency across different paragraphs. NoisySumm distills the knowledge in a noisy teacher model into a student model.

However these models suffer from hallucinations because they cannot ensure that the generated summaries are factually correct. Hallucinations are the nonsensical or unfaithful contents in generated texts. They can hinder performance and introduce false information in real-world applications. For example in Figure 1, the summarization model gets the band name and band genre of the given entity Peter Wichers right, but it wrongly assumes the nationality is American instead of Sweden. The model is hallucinated by the text snippet “from Atlanta and Baltimore” in the source, and it mistakenly relates this snippet to the nationality of America, ignoring the fact that Peter Wichers comes from Sweden. Factual errors like these are hard to detect with automatic metrics and they can degrade the system performance, which leads to failing to meet user expectations in real-world scenarios.

Hallucination is an intrinsic drawback of language models, and it is challenging even for large language models. It is difficult to eliminate hallucinations under the traditional sequence-to-sequence paradigm, and there have been different attempts to bring in external knowledge, like dense retrieval or API calling. Templates are naturally suitable for using external knowledge, because the slots in templates can guide the retrieval of knowledge. Template-based methods are widely used in different text generation problems like data-to-text and dialogue system, but there are no template-based solutions for entity abstract summarization yet. Since it is difficult to locate hallucinations in plain text, we augment the language model so that it generates semi-structured templates before it outputs the final summary. We view the entity abstract as a combination of Facts and Template. Facts is the factual information about the given entity, and Template is the remaining generic components. This way we can easily locate the facts in the generated summaries, and correct wrong predictions with external knowledge like a knowledge base or human assistance.

Based on this facts-template decomposition, in this paper we propose SlotSum, an explainable entity abstract summarization framework that disentangles facts from the generated entity abstracts in order to reduce hallucination. First SlotSum generates a template from the input documents, where the facts in the template are replaced by slots that are marked with special tokens. Then SlotSum predicts the facts for each slot, and tries to rectify the predictions with credible external knowledge. The final summary is built by filling the facts into the slots. SlotSum can ensure factual correctness by bringing in external knowledge sources, but it still keeps the ability to generate summaries only from the input documents. The framework is also highly controllable and explainable, because the facts are stated explicitly and can be edited easily.

We supplement the WikiSum dataset with related facts and construct WikiFactSum, so that we can observe the effectiveness of disentangling facts. SlotSum with BART-large as the backbone model clearly outperforms other baseline models on ROUGE score when credible external knowledge is given. We also evaluate factual correctness with both automatic metrics and human evaluation, and SlotSum provides significantly more correct facts.

To sum up, the main contributions of our work are:

- We disentangle fact from the generated text in the entity abstract summarization task, which helps reduce the hallucinations produced by pretrained language models.

- We propose SlotSum, an entity abstract summarization framework that first generates templates with slots, then predicts facts and corrects them further with external knowledge to fill in the slots.

- We construct a new dataset WikiFactSum and run a series of experiments on it. SlotSum shows a clear advantage over other baseline models, which indicates that disentangling facts from the text leads to more factually correct summaries.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Entity abstract summarization aims to generate a correct and fluent summary of an entity based on a collection of relevant documents gathered from the Internet. The task is typically viewed as a variant of the multi-document summarization task, as illustrated in Figure 1. Entity abstract summarization could provide users with condensed information about a given entity in search engines, and assist the writing of new Wikipedia entries [1].

Early work [1,2] on entity abstract summarization generally adopts extractive methods that select valuable sentences from the input documents, which suffer from poor fluency in the generated summary. Inspired by the large-scale WikiSum [3] dataset, recent work tends to directly generate abstractive summaries from the given input documents. Various approaches have been explored to identify the necessary information from the vast input documents: [4] classifies documents into different topics to filter out noisy data, HierSumm [5] ranks the input documents with a learning-based ranker and models the dependency across different paragraphs, and NoisySumm [6] distills the knowledge in a noisy teacher model into a student model.

However, these models suffer from hallucinations, as they are not able to ensure the factual correctness of the generated summaries. Hallucinations refer to nonsensical or unfaithful contents in the generated texts [7]. They could hinder performance and introduce false information in real-world applications [8]. Taking Figure 1 as an example, the summarization model correctly identifies the band name and band genre of the given entity Peter Wichers, but incorrectly assumes the nationality to be American rather than Sweden. Hallucinated by the text snippet “from Atlanta and Baltimore” in the source, the model mistakenly relates the snippet to the nationality of America, ignoring the fact that Peter Wichers comes from Sweden. Such factual errors are difficult to detect with automatic metrics and could degrade system performance, leading to a failure to meet user expectations in real-world scenarios [8].

Hallucination is an intrinsic drawback of language models and remains challenging even for large language models [9]. Hallucinations are hard to eliminate under the traditional sequence-to-sequence paradigm, and various attempts have been made to introduce external knowledge such as dense retrieval [10] or API calling [11]. Templates are naturally suited to utilising external knowledge, as the slots in templates can provide guidance for retrieving knowledge. While template-based methods are widely adopted in text generation problems like data-to-text [12] and dialogue system [13], there are not yet template-based solutions for entity abstract summarization. To address the difficulty of locating hallucinations in plain text, we augment the language model to generate semi-structured templates before outputting the final summary. We view the entity abstract as a combination of Facts and Template, where Facts represents the factual information about the given entity, and Template represents the remaining generic components. In this way, we can easily locate the facts in generated summaries and correct erroneous predictions with external knowledge such as a knowledge base or human assistance.

Based on the facts-template decomposition, we propose SlotSum, an explainable entity abstract summarization framework that disentangles facts from generated entity abstracts to reduce hallucination. SlotSum first generates a template according to the input documents, in which the facts are replaced by slots marked with special tokens. It then predicts the facts for each slot and attempts to rectify the predictions with credible external knowledge. The final summary is constructed by filling the facts into the slots. SlotSum can ensure factual correctness by introducing external knowledge sources, while retaining the ability to generate summaries solely from the input documents. Moreover, the framework is highly controllable and explainable, since the facts are explicitly stated and can be easily edited.

By supplementing the WikiSum [3] dataset with related facts, we construct WikiFactSum to observe the effectiveness of disentangling facts. SlotSum, with BART-large [14] as the backbone model, clearly outperforms the other baseline models on ROUGE score when credible external knowledge is provided. We also evaluate factual correctness with both automatic metrics and human evaluation, where SlotSum provides significantly more correct facts.

In summary, the main contributions of our work are as follows:

- • We disentangle facts from the generated text in the entity abstract summarization task, which helps to reduce hallucinations produced by pretrained language models.

- • We propose SlotSum, an entity abstract summarization framework that first generates templates with slots, then predicts facts and corrects them with external knowledge to fill in the slots.

- • We construct a new dataset, WikiFactSum, and conduct a series of experiments on it. SlotSum demonstrates a clear advantage over the other baseline models, indicating that disentangling facts from the text leads to more factually correct summaries.
